rejected.title: Comparing voice across texts
card: Voice is the personality a reader hears in a text. It comes from word choice, sentence length and the speaker's attitude to the subject.
To compare voices, keep the subject the same and look at what differs. Ask which words, which sentence shapes and which attitude each writer chose.
Take two speakers describing the same empty house. One says, "The house sat hollow, and I missed every room." The other says, "The house was vacant. Sold by Friday."
The first voice uses a warm, longing word ("missed") and a flowing sentence, so a reader feels sadness. The second uses short, flat sentences and a businesslike tone, so a reader feels distance.
rejected.remember: Same subject, different choices of word, sentence and attitude, different feelings in the reader.

a.q: Two poems describe the same storm. One uses long, rolling sentences and calls it a "magnificent roar". The other uses short, clipped sentences and calls it a "nuisance". What does comparing them show?
opts: Different language choices create different feelings
Both poems give the reader the same feelings
Longer sentences make a poem better written
The storm itself changes between the two poems
a.why: The subject is the same, but the word choices and sentence lengths differ, so one voice feels awed and the other feels annoyed. The option about better writing is wrong because comparing voice is about effect, not quality.
a.clue: Keep the subject fixed and ask what changed.

b.q: Two narrators describe the first day at a new school. Narrator A says, "Heart thudding, I froze. Could everyone see me shake?" Narrator B says, "First day. Bag down. Seat found. Fine." How do the voices differ in effect?
opts: A sounds anxious and open, B sounds guarded
A sounds confident and calm, B sounds nervous
A and B sound equally anxious, B uses fewer words
A sounds cold and distant, B sounds warm
b.why: A names signs of fear, "thudding" and "shake", and asks a worried question, so the reader hears nerves shared openly. B uses clipped fragments and the flat word "Fine", which sounds controlled and may hold feeling back. The option saying both are equally anxious ignores how B's short, flat sentences change the attitude.
b.clue: Look at what each narrator admits to feeling, and how.
